title: How to Cheer Someone Up: 25 Easy Ways to Make Them Smile
h1: How to Cheer Someone Up: 25 Easy, Thoughtful Ways to Make Them Smile
description: Learn how to cheer someone up with 25 thoughtful ideas, from listening well to small surprises, plus what to say, what to avoid and when to get help.
excerpt: Twenty-five thoughtful ways to cheer someone up, in person or from afar, plus what to say, what to skip and how to tell when they need more than a pep talk.
intro:
When someone you care about is having a rough day, it’s natural to want to fix it right away. But cheering someone up isn’t about forcing a smile onto their face. It’s about helping them feel less alone with whatever they’re carrying, and then, gently, reminding them that good things still exist.

This guide covers how to cheer someone up in a way that actually feels supportive: how to listen first, what to say (and what to avoid), and 25 practical ideas for partners, friends and family, whether you’re in the same room or texting from across the country. You’ll also learn how to spot when someone needs more than a pick-me-up.
body:
Start by listening, not fixing

The fastest way to help someone feel better is often the least flashy: let them talk. People usually need to feel understood before they can feel uplifted.

  • Ask an open question. “Do you want to talk about it?” or “What’s been going on?” gives them room without pressure.
  • Reflect what you hear. “That sounds really frustrating” shows you’re paying attention.
  • Ask what they need. “Do you want advice, a distraction, or just someone to vent to?” This one question prevents a lot of well-meaning misses.
  • Get comfortable with silence. You don’t have to fill every pause.
Tip: If they choose “just vent,” resist the urge to solve the problem. Nodding along and saying “that makes sense” can be more comforting than the perfect solution.

What to say when someone is feeling down

You don’t need a speech. Simple, sincere words work best:

  • “I’m here for you, whatever you need.”
  • “You don’t have to go through this by yourself.”
  • “It makes total sense that you feel this way.”
  • “I’m proud of you for handling as much as you have.”
  • “Want me to come over, or would you rather have some space?”

What to avoid saying

  • “It could be worse.” It shrinks their feelings rather than easing them.
  • “Just think positive.” Optimism helps, but only after someone feels heard.
  • “I know exactly how you feel.” Share your experience if it helps, but keep the focus on them.
  • Comparisons. Their hard day doesn’t need to compete with anyone else’s.

25 ways to cheer someone up in person

Comfort and care

  1. Make them a warm drink. A cup of tea, cocoa or their favorite coffee order is a small ritual that says “I’m taking care of you.”
  2. Cook or bring their comfort food. Mac and cheese, soup, a favorite takeout order. Food is love in a very practical form.
  3. Handle a chore. Do the dishes, walk the dog or run an errand so they have one less thing to worry about.
  4. Offer a hug if they want one. Ask first. Some people find touch comforting; others need space.
  5. Set up a cozy corner. Blankets, pillows, a candle and a favorite show can turn a bad evening into a restful one.

A change of scenery

  1. Take a walk outside. Fresh air and movement often shift a mood, even a little.
  2. Go for a drive with a good playlist. Windows down, singing optional.
  3. Visit a favorite spot. A park, a bookstore, a coffee shop with good memories.
  4. Browse a store together. Window shopping, a thrift store treasure hunt or a farmers market. It’s about the outing, not the spending.
  5. Try something new together. A pottery class, a new cafe or a short hike gives their brain something fresh to focus on.

Laughter and lightness

  1. Watch a comedy you both love. Familiar favorites are especially comforting.
  2. Look through funny old photos. Shared memories bring smiles fast.
  3. Play a silly game. Cards, a video game or a round of our challenges to do at home.
  4. Send them the meme that perfectly sums up their day. Being seen, even through a joke, helps.
  5. Have a dance break. Put on an upbeat song and be ridiculous together.

Thoughtful gestures

  1. Write a note. List a few things you love about them or remind them of a time they overcame something hard.
  2. Give a small, meaningful gift. Flowers, their favorite snack, a book you think they’ll like.
  3. Make them a playlist. Songs that remind you of them or that you know lift their spirits.
  4. Plan something to look forward to. A day trip, a concert or a simple dinner next week gives them a bright spot on the horizon.
  5. Remind them of their strengths. Specific praise sticks: “You handled that client with so much patience.”

How to cheer someone up from a distance

Distance doesn’t mean you can’t help. A little effort goes a long way.

  1. Send a voice note. Hearing a familiar voice feels more personal than text.
  2. Schedule a video call. Watch a show together, eat dinner “together” or just chat.
  3. Have something delivered. Their favorite meal, a care package or flowers.
  4. Text a sweet good-morning message. Something to wake up to can set a kinder tone for the day. Our cute paragraphs to wake up to offer inspiration.
  5. Check in again tomorrow. Following up shows your support isn’t a one-time thing.

Tailoring your approach to the person

What helps one person might annoy another. Think about who they are:

  • Introverts may appreciate quiet company, a thoughtful message or space to recharge rather than a big outing.
  • Extroverts may perk up with a social plan or a lively conversation.
  • Partners may want physical affection and reassurance. Our guide on how to show someone you love them has more ideas.
  • People going through a breakup may need patience and distraction in equal measure. See how to deal with a breakup for ways to support them.

When in doubt, ask. “What usually helps you when you feel like this?” is a caring question, not an awkward one.

Quick pick-me-ups when you only have five minutes

You don’t always have an evening to spare. These tiny gestures still make a difference on a busy day:

  • Send a photo of something that reminded you of them.
  • Leave a sticky note on their mirror, laptop or lunch bag.
  • Order their favorite coffee to be ready when they arrive.
  • Text a specific memory: “Remember when we got lost and found that amazing taco truck?”
  • Tell them one thing you admire about how they handle tough situations.
  • Share a song with a note that says, “This made me think of you.”

Small, frequent kindnesses add up. Often what people remember isn’t a grand gesture but the fact that someone thought of them when things were hard.

Be optimistic without dismissing their feelings

Hope is a powerful gift, as long as it comes after empathy. Once they feel heard, you can gently offer perspective: “This is really hard right now, and I also believe you’ll get through it.” That combination of validation and confidence helps people feel both understood and encouraged.

When someone needs more than cheering up

Sometimes sadness goes deeper than a bad day. Pay attention if someone you love has felt low for weeks, has stopped enjoying things they used to love, is withdrawing from everyone, or talks about feeling hopeless.

Tip: Encourage them, kindly, to talk to a doctor or licensed therapist, and offer to help them find one. If they mention wanting to hurt themselves, stay with them and call or text 988 (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US), or call 911 in an emergency.

You can still be a warm, steady presence while they get professional support. You don’t have to be their only source of help, and you shouldn’t try to be.

Take care of yourself, too

Supporting someone can be draining, especially over a long stretch. Keep up your own routines, lean on your own friends and set gentle limits when you need to. You’ll be more helpful from a full cup than an empty one. If you’re feeling isolated yourself, our guide on how to deal with loneliness may help.

The bottom line

Knowing how to cheer someone up comes down to three things: listen first, show up in practical ways, and remind them they’re not alone. A warm drink, a walk, a silly movie or a heartfelt note can turn a heavy day into a slightly lighter one, and that’s often exactly enough.
takeaways: Listen first and ask whether they want advice, distraction or just support.
Small, practical gestures like a warm drink or a handled chore mean a lot.
Avoid minimizing phrases like “it could be worse” or “just think positive.”
From a distance, voice notes, deliveries and follow-up check-ins help.
If sadness lasts for weeks, gently encourage professional support.

faq.q: What do you text someone to cheer them up?
faq.a: Keep it simple and sincere: “Thinking of you today, I’m here if you want to talk,” or “I know things are hard, and I’m proud of how you’re handling it.” A funny meme or a shared memory can add lightness once they feel heard. Follow up the next day to show you care.

faq.q: How do you cheer someone up without being annoying?
faq.a: Ask what they need instead of guessing, respect it if they want space, and avoid pushing positivity too early. Offer specific help rather than vague offers, and keep check-ins short and warm. Being present without pressure is usually what people appreciate most.

faq.q: How do you cheer up a friend who is sad?
faq.a: Listen without judgment, validate their feelings, then offer a gentle change of pace like a walk, a favorite movie or comfort food. Remind them of their strengths and plan something to look forward to. If the sadness lingers for weeks, encourage them to talk to a professional.

faq.q: How can I cheer up my partner after a bad day?
faq.a: Give them a moment to decompress, then ask how their day went and really listen. Take a chore off their plate, offer physical comfort if they want it, and plan a cozy evening. Small acts of care often mean more than big gestures when someone is worn out.
